chapter.name: Tales by Dots and Lines
chapter.blurb: The mean and median as a 'balancing point' of data -- how they change when a value is added, removed, or when every value is shifted or scaled by a fixed number; finding an unknown value given the mean; finding the mean and median of frequency-table data; basic spreadsheet cell references and SUM/AVERAGE formulas; and reading, comparing and interpreting line graphs of data that changes over time.

scope_in.item: The mean as a 'balancing point': the sum of the distances of values below it equals the sum of distances of values above it, and why there is only one such centre
How the mean changes when a value greater than, less than, or equal to it is included in or removed from the data
Finding combinations of values that can be included in or removed from the data without changing the mean
How the mean changes when a fixed number is added to, subtracted from, or multiplied with every value in the data, proved algebraically using x1, x2, ..., xn
How the median changes when a value greater than or less than it is included in the data
Finding an unknown/missing value in a data set given its mean and the other values, including correcting a data set for a recording error
Finding the mean and median of data presented in a frequency table, using value times frequency and cumulative frequency to locate the median's position
Reading and writing basic spreadsheet cell references (e.g. E5), range notation (Start:End, e.g. B3:G3), and SUM/AVERAGE formulas
Figure It Out problems on mean and median: reverse problems, dot plots, and true/sometimes/never justification of statements about how mean and median change
Reading a line graph: identifying axes, scale and what each line represents (Step 1), then inferring and interpreting trends and comparisons (Step 2)
Why a line graph is preferred over a clustered-column graph for data with many points that changes over time
Reading and comparing multiple lines on the same line graph (e.g. monthly rainfall across several cities)
The chapter's summary statements on the balancing property of mean and median, and on line graphs showing change over time

concepts.name: Mean and median as a balancing centre: effect of including or removing a value
concepts.description: How the mean and median change when a value greater than, less than, or equal to them is included in or removed from a data set.
concepts.idea: The mean is the point where the total distance of values below it equals the total distance of values above it, so including a value greater than the mean pulls the mean up and including one less than the mean pulls it down; the median moves the same way when a value is included.
concepts.rule: For a data set with mean m: including a new value greater than m makes the new mean greater than m; including a value less than m makes the new mean less than m; including a value equal to m leaves the mean unchanged. Removing a value works the opposite way -- removing a value greater than the mean decreases the mean, and removing a value less than the mean increases it. Two or more values can be included or removed together, some above and some below the current mean, so that their effects cancel and the mean stays the same. The median moves the same way: including a value greater than the current median increases the median, and including a value less than it decreases the median.
concepts.example: The data 10, 10, 11, 17 has mean 12. Including the value 20 (greater than 12) raises the mean to 13.6. Including the value 5 (less than 12) lowers the mean to 10.6.

questions.q: A student claims: 'If I remove the largest value from a data set, the mean will always decrease.' Using the data 4, 6, 8, 50 (mean 17), check whether removing the largest value (50) decreases the mean, and then decide whether the student's claim is true in general. Justify using the balancing rule for the mean.
questions.a: Removing 50 leaves 4, 6, 8 with mean 6, which is less than 17, confirming the claim in this example. In general, the largest value in a data set is always greater than or equal to the mean, so removing it must decrease the mean, by the rule that removing a value greater than the mean decreases it -- true whenever the values are not all equal. If every value in the data set is equal, the largest value equals the mean, and removing it does not change the mean at all.
s: Computes that removing 50 from 4, 6, 8, 50 gives mean 6, less than the original mean 17, confirming the claim in this example

concepts.name: Effect on the mean of a fixed change applied to every value
concepts.description: How the mean changes when a fixed number is added to, subtracted from, or multiplied with every value in a data set, proved algebraically.
concepts.idea: If every value of a data set is increased, decreased, or scaled by the same fixed number, the mean changes in exactly the same way -- add k to every value and the mean increases by k; multiply every value by k and the mean is multiplied by k.
concepts.rule: If a data set has mean a and every value has a fixed number k added to it, the new mean is a + k. If every value has k subtracted, the new mean is a - k. If every value is multiplied by a fixed number k, the new mean is a * k. This follows from writing the mean as (x1+x2+...+xn)/n = a and applying the operation to each xi inside the sum.
concepts.example: The data 2, 4, 6 has mean 4. Adding 10 to every value gives 12, 14, 16, with mean 14 = 4 + 10. Multiplying every value by 3 gives 6, 12, 18, with mean 12 = 4 * 3.

concepts.name: Finding an unknown value in a data set from its mean
concepts.description: Finding a missing value in a data set from its mean and the other known values, including correcting a data set for a recording error.
concepts.idea: When the mean of a data set and all but one value are known, the missing value can be found by first finding the total sum (mean times number of values) and then subtracting the sum of the known values.
concepts.rule: If a data set of n values has mean m, the sum of all values is m times n. Given n-1 of the values, the missing value equals (m times n) minus the sum of the known values. The same reverse-reasoning approach can correct a data set for a recording error: subtract or add the size of the error to the recorded total, then divide by the number of values to get the corrected mean.
concepts.example: Ten wrestlers' weights have mean 39.2 kg, and nine of them sum to 349 kg. The tenth weight is 39.2 x 10 - 349 = 43 kg.

concepts.name: Mean and median of data in a frequency table
concepts.description: Finding the mean and median of data organised in a frequency table, using value times frequency and cumulative frequency.
concepts.idea: When many values repeat, a frequency table lists each distinct value with how many times it occurs; the mean is found by weighting each value by its frequency, and the median is found by locating the middle position(s) using running totals of the frequencies.
concepts.rule: For data in a frequency table, mean = (sum of value times frequency for every row) divided by (sum of all frequencies). To find the median, add up the frequencies in order until the running total first reaches or passes the position(s) of the middle value(s); the value in that row is the median (for an even total count, the median is the average of the two middle values, if they fall in different rows).
concepts.example: Family sizes 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10 have frequencies 3, 11, 9, 7, 3, 1, 1, 1 (total 36). The mean is 188/36 = 5.22, and the median (average of the 18th and 19th positions) is 5.

concepts.name: Spreadsheet cell references, ranges and SUM/AVERAGE formulas
concepts.description: Cell references, range notation, and the SUM and AVERAGE formulas used in a spreadsheet to total and average data.
concepts.idea: A spreadsheet organises data into cells named by a column letter and row number; a range of cells in a row or column is written as Start:End, and formulas such as SUM and AVERAGE let a computer add up or average many cells at once instead of doing it by hand.
concepts.rule: A cell is named by its column letter followed by its row number, e.g. E5 is in column E, row 5. A range of consecutive cells in one row or column is written Start:End, e.g. B3:G3 for row 3 from column B to G, or D2:D6 for column D from row 2 to 6. The formula =SUM(range) adds up all values in the range; =AVERAGE(range) finds their mean.
concepts.example: If Nagesh's marks across 6 subjects are in cells B3 to G3, then =SUM(B3:G3) gives his total marks and =AVERAGE(B3:G3) gives his average mark.

concepts.name: Reading and interpreting line graphs
concepts.description: Reading a line graph's axes and scale, and drawing valid inferences and comparisons from the trend it shows.
concepts.idea: A line graph plots values against time and connects them with line segments, making it easy to see how a quantity rises, falls, or stays steady, and to compare two or more trends on the same graph.
concepts.rule: On a line graph, the horizontal axis usually shows time (or another ordered variable) and the vertical axis shows the quantity being measured; a steeper line segment means a faster rate of change than a flatter one. Reading a line graph has two steps: Step 1 -- identify what is given (axes, scale, how many lines/colours, what each represents); Step 2 -- infer and interpret (state observations and conclusions that the graph's data actually supports, without assuming information the graph doesn't show). Line graphs suit data that changes over time better than column/bar graphs, especially when there are many time points, because connecting points with lines keeps the picture uncluttered.
concepts.example: A line graph of monthly maximum temperature in two states lets you read off each state's highest and lowest month, and compare how much each one's temperature varies across the year, just from the shape and steepness of the two lines.
